readings.title: A Visit From St. Nicholas
readings.author: Clement Clarke Moore
readings.challenge: See the night through the eyes of someone who can hardly believe what he is watching, and listen for the galloping beat.
readings.focus: On Christmas Eve a father, woken by a clatter, watches St. Nicholas arrive by flying sleigh, fill the stockings and fly away.
readings.context: Mary E. Burt, a New York teacher, gathered the poems her pupils loved best in Poems That Every Child Should Know (1904); this reading follows its 1907 printing. This poem was first printed in a New York newspaper in 1823 with no author’s name. It is usually credited to Clement Clarke Moore (1779–1863), a New York professor who later printed it among his poems, and it did much to shape how Americans picture Santa Claus. A ’kerchief is a cloth tied over the hair for sleeping; the sash is the window frame that slides up; luster is shine; coursers are swift horses, here the reindeer; a peddler sells things from a pack on his back; droll means funny; an elf is a small magical person. Donder and Blitzen mean thunder and lightning. The slanted words are names, as the book prints them.

excerpt.locator: “A Visit From St. Nicholas,” the whole poem; opens “’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring,…”; closes “…exclaim, ere he drove out of sight, “_Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good-night_.””.

questions.prompt: What is everyone in the house doing when the poem begins? What wakes the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone is still: the children are asleep dreaming of sugar-plums, and the speaker and mamma have just settled down for the night. A clatter out on the lawn sends him running to the window.
evidence: Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse;
When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter,

questions.prompt: Find the words that make St. Nicholas small and quick, and the words that make him jolly. Does he look the way you picture Santa Claus?
facilitatorNotes: He drives a “miniature sleigh” with “eight tiny reindeer” and is “a little old driver, so lively and quick”; he is “a right jolly old elf” with a round belly that shakes like jelly. Here he is elf-sized and covered in soot, more like a peddler than a grand figure; children can compare him with pictures they know.
evidence: But a miniature sleigh, and eight tiny reindeer,
With a little old driver, so lively and quick,
He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf,

questions.prompt: Moore compares the reindeer flying up to the house-top with dry leaves in a hurricane. How are they alike?
facilitatorNotes: When blowing leaves hit something in their way, the wind lifts them up into the sky. The reindeer rise to the roof just as quickly and lightly, as if a great wind swept them up.
evidence: As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly,
When they meet with an obstacle, mount to the sky;

questions.prompt: St. Nicholas says nothing until he is leaving. How does the speaker know he has “nothing to dread”? Why might Moore keep the visitor silent until the very end?
facilitatorNotes: A wink and a twist of the head tell him the visitor is friendly. Working without a word keeps him mysterious and busy, and makes his one sentence at the end, a good wish for everyone, the last thing we hear.
evidence: A wink of his eye and a twist of his head,
Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread;
He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work,

readings.title: Little Orphant Annie
readings.author: James Whitcomb Riley
readings.challenge: Read a poem written the way a child talks, and let its goblin tales give you a shiver.
readings.focus: A hired orphan girl tells the farm children goblin tales about naughty children who vanished, and ends with advice on how to be safe.
readings.context: Mary E. Burt, a New York teacher, gathered the poems her pupils loved best in Poems That Every Child Should Know (1904); this reading follows its 1907 printing. James Whitcomb Riley (1849–1916) was called the Hoosier Poet because he wrote about his home state of Indiana, often in the country talk of its people; this poem was first printed in 1885. An orphan might then be taken into a farm family to work for her “board-an’-keep,” her meals and a bed. Gobble-uns are goblins. The spellings show how the child speaker talks: ’at means “that,” thist means “just,” onc’t means “once,” kivvers are covers, chimbly is chimney, ’ud allus means “would always,” he’p is help, churish is cherish, and squenched means put out. A roundabout is a short jacket; a press is a cupboard. Halloween is a night for scary stories by the fire.
readings.contentNote: In Annie’s tales, children who misbehave are carried off by goblins and “Black Things.” The stories are meant as shivery fun.

excerpt.locator: “Little Orphant Annie,” the whole poem; opens “Little Orphant Annie’s come to our house to stay, An’ wash the cups and saucers up, an’…”; closes “…needy ones ’at clusters all about, Er the Gobble-uns’ll git you Ef you Don’t Watch Out!”.

questions.prompt: What jobs does Annie do at the farm? What happens when the supper things are done?
facilitatorNotes: She washes the cups and saucers, brushes away crumbs, shoos the chickens, dusts, sweeps, makes the fire and bakes the bread. Then the children sit around the kitchen fire and listen to her witch-tales.
evidence: An’ make the fire, an’ bake the bread, an’ earn her board-an’-keep;
A-list’nin’ to the witch-tales ’at Annie tells about,

questions.prompt: What did the little boy and the little girl in Annie’s stories do wrong, and what happened to each?
facilitatorNotes: The boy would not say his prayers, and when his parents turned down his covers he was gone; only his pants and jacket were found. The girl laughed at everyone and mocked the company, and two great Black Things snatched her up through the ceiling.
evidence: Onc’t they was a little boy wouldn’t say his pray’rs--
But all they ever found was thist his pants an’ roundabout!
They was two great big Black Things a-standin’ by her side,

questions.prompt: Look at the end of each stanza, where the words step across the page one at a time: “Ef you / Don’t / Watch / Out!” How should they be read aloud? Why might Riley set them out this way?
facilitatorNotes: Slowly, one word at a time and getting quieter or more spooky, then a jump on “Out!” The steps across the page are like footsteps creeping closer, so listeners wait for the scare.
evidence: An’ the Gobble-uns ’at gits you
Er the Gobble-uns’ll git you

questions.prompt: In the last stanza Annie tells how to be safe from the Gobble-uns. What does she say to do? Why might an orphan, of all people, add “dry the orphant’s tear”?
facilitatorNotes: Mind your parents and teachers, cherish the people who love you, help the poor and needy, and dry the orphan’s tear. Annie is an orphan herself, working for her keep, so her spooky tale ends by asking for kindness to children like her. Some children will think she is only finishing a good story; others may feel her own loneliness in it.
evidence: An’ churish them ’at loves you, an’ dry the orphant’s tear,
An’ he’p the pore an’ needy ones ’at clusters all about,

readings.title: The Death of the Old Year
readings.author: Alfred Tennyson
readings.workTitle: The Death of the Old Year
readings.challenge: Hear the year spoken of as a person, and follow his last hour.
readings.focus: On New Year’s Eve friends sit by the bed of the dying Old Year, remember the good times, and open the door to the new one.
readings.context: Mary E. Burt, a New York teacher, gathered the poems her pupils loved best in Poems That Every Child Should Know (1904); this reading follows its 1907 printing. Alfred Tennyson (1809–1892) was the most famous English poet of his time; he published this poem in 1832. It imagines the last hour of the year, at midnight on December 31, as the deathbed of an old friend; on New Year’s Day the new year has just come in. To toll a bell is to ring it slowly, as for a funeral; to froth bumpers to the brim is to fill cups until they foam over, at a party; quips are jokes; post-haste means as fast as possible; rue means to be sorry; blithe means cheerful. Lieth, doth, hath and standeth are old forms of lies, does, has and stands.
readings.contentNote: The poem describes a death, with the old custom of closing a dead person’s eyes and tying up the chin. It also mentions cups of drink at a party.

excerpt.locator: “The Death of the Old Year,” by Alfred Tennyson, the whole poem; opens “Full knee-deep lies the winter snow, And the winter winds are wearily sighing: Toll ye…”; closes “…on the floor, my friend, And a new face at the door, my friend, A new face at the door.”.

questions.prompt: Who is dying in this poem? How can you tell he is not a real old man?
facilitatorNotes: The old year. He has lived with the speakers for a year, he dies as the clock comes to twelve on New Year’s Eve, and his “son and heir,” the New-year, rides up to take his place.
evidence: For the old year lies a-dying.
’Tis nearly twelve o’clock.
His son and heir doth ride post-haste,

questions.prompt: What do the speakers remember about the Old Year? Find something he gave them and something they did together.
facilitatorNotes: He gave a friend and a true love; he was jolly, full of jokes, and filled the cups at parties; they laughed and cried together. He was a good friend even if others speak ill of him.
evidence: He gave me a friend, and a true true-love,
He was full of joke and jest,
We did so laugh and cry with you,

questions.prompt: Each stanza ends with a short indented song. How do these little songs change from the first stanza to the last?
facilitatorNotes: At first the speakers refuse: “you shall not die.” Then they half accept it: “if you must die.” Then they say goodbye and ask him to speak. In the last stanza they turn to the newcomer: a new foot on the floor and a new face at the door.
evidence: Old year, you shall not die.
Old year, if you must die.
There’s a new foot on the floor, my friend,

questions.prompt: The speaker worries that the New-year “will take ’em away,” the friend and the true love. Why might someone feel sad, and not only happy, when a new year begins? Is the ending sad or hopeful?
facilitatorNotes: A year holds people and memories, and change can take them away; the new year is a stranger. But the newcomer is “blithe and bold,” cheerful and brave, and waiting to be let in. Children may hear the ending as sad, hopeful, or both.
evidence: And the New-year will take ’em away.
And the New-year blithe and bold, my friend,
And a new face at the door, my friend,

readings.title: The Battle of Blenheim
readings.author: Robert Southey
readings.challenge: Listen to the children’s questions and the old man’s answers, and notice what he can and cannot explain.
readings.focus: Two children find a skull by a stream, and their grandfather tells them about the famous battle fought there long ago.
readings.context: Mary E. Burt, a New York teacher, gathered the poems her pupils loved best in Poems That Every Child Should Know (1904); this reading follows its 1907 printing. Robert Southey (1774–1843) was an English poet; he wrote this poem in 1798. The Battle of Blenheim was fought in 1704 near the village of Blenheim, in what is now Germany, when an English army led by the Duke of Marlborough and an Austrian army led by Prince Eugene beat the French. In the poem an old farmer, Kaspar, lives on the battlefield many years later. A rivulet is a little stream; a plowshare is the blade of a plow; to put an army to rout is to make it run away; a childing mother is a mother about to have a baby; quoth means said. Veterans Day, November 11, honors people who have served in war and remembers what war costs.
readings.contentNote: Kaspar tells of thousands of soldiers killed, a family’s home burned, and mothers and babies who died; the children find a skull from the battle.

excerpt.locator: “The Battle of Blenheim,” by Robert Southey, the whole poem; opens “It was a summer’s evening, Old Kaspar’s work was done, And he before his cottage door Was…”; closes “…Quoth little Peterkin. “Why, that I cannot tell,” said he, “But ’twas a famous victory.””.

questions.prompt: What does Peterkin find by the stream? How does Kaspar know what it is, and why might he sigh?
facilitatorNotes: A skull, round and smooth. Kaspar finds them often, in his garden and when he plows, because thousands of men were killed there. His sigh shows he has seen this many times and it still saddens him.
evidence: Roll something large and round,
’Tis some poor fellow’s skull
The plowshare turns them out;

questions.prompt: The children ask what the war was “all about” and “what they killed each other for.” What does Kaspar answer?
facilitatorNotes: He knows who won: the English beat the French. But he cannot explain why they fought; he only repeats that everybody said it was a famous victory.
evidence: I could not well make out.
That ’twas a famous victory!

questions.prompt: What happened to Kaspar’s own family and to the people of the countryside? How does Kaspar explain these things?
facilitatorNotes: His father’s house was burned and the family fled with nowhere to sleep; the land was wasted by fire and sword, and mothers and new babies died. Kaspar says such things “must be” at every famous victory, as if he has been told that and never questioned it.
evidence: They burned his dwelling to the ground
And new-born baby died.
But things like that, you know, must be

questions.prompt: Wilhelmine says, “Why, ’twas a very wicked thing!” and Peterkin asks, “But what good came of it at last?” Who seems wiser here, the children or the old man? What do you think Southey wanted readers to think about war?
facilitatorNotes: The children ask simple questions the grown-ups never answered; Kaspar can only say “famous victory.” Southey seems to want readers to ask whether glory is worth so many lives when no one can say what good came of it. Some children may feel sorry for Kaspar, who is honest about not knowing. Remembering what war costs is part of honoring those who fight.
evidence: Why, ’twas a very wicked thing!
But what good came of it at last?
Why, that I cannot tell

readings.title: America
readings.author: Samuel Francis Smith
readings.challenge: Work out who “I,” “we” and “thee” are in a song that a whole country sings together.
readings.focus: A song of love for the country and its freedom, meant to be sung by everyone at once.
readings.context: Mary E. Burt, a New York teacher, gathered the poems her pupils loved best in Poems That Every Child Should Know (1904); this reading follows its 1907 printing. Samuel Francis Smith (1808–1895) wrote “America,” often called “My Country, ’Tis of Thee,” in 1831 while he was studying to be a minister, and children first sang it in Boston on the Fourth of July that year. It uses the tune of Britain’s “God Save the King,” and for many years Americans sang it as a national anthem. Independence Day, July 4, remembers the Declaration of Independence of 1776. Rills are little streams; templed hills are hills with churches on them; rapture is great joy; to partake is to take part; mortal tongues are human voices. When Smith wrote, slavery was still legal in much of the country, so many people did not yet share the freedom the song praises.

excerpt.locator: “America,” by Samuel Francis Smith, the whole song; opens “My country, ’tis of thee, Sweet land of liberty, Of thee I sing; Land where my fathers…”; closes “…land be bright With freedom’s holy light: Protect us by Thy might, Great God, our King.”.

questions.prompt: List the parts of the land the song names. Which of them can you see, and which can you not see?
facilitatorNotes: Mountainsides, rocks, rills, woods, templed hills, the breeze and the trees can be seen and heard. Liberty, freedom and pride cannot be seen; the song joins them to the land, so that freedom rings from every mountain.
evidence: I love thy rocks and rills,
From every mountain side,
Let freedom ring.

questions.prompt: In the third stanza, who and what are asked to join the song?
facilitatorNotes: The breeze, the trees, every human voice, everything that breathes, and even the silent rocks. The whole land is asked to sing.
evidence: And ring from all the trees
Let all that breathe partake;
Let rocks their silence break--

questions.prompt: “Land where my fathers died, / Land of the Pilgrims’ pride.” Who are the “fathers”? Could every person who sings this song say these words about their own family?
facilitatorNotes: The fathers are the people who came before: ancestors such as the Pilgrims and those who died making the country. Many Americans’ families came later, or lived here long before the Pilgrims, or were brought by force; they still sing the line, as a country’s shared story. Children can talk about whose story the line tells and whose it leaves out.
evidence: Land where my fathers died,
Land of the Pilgrims’ pride;

questions.prompt: The song begins “Of thee I sing” and ends “To Thee we sing.” Who is “thee” at the start, and who is “Thee” at the end? Why might the song change from “I” to “we”?
facilitatorNotes: At the start it is the country; at the end it is God, called the “Author of liberty.” One singer becomes a whole crowd, as on the Fourth of July when people sing together; freedom is shared, so the song ends with everyone.
evidence: Of thee I sing;
To Thee we sing:
Author of liberty,
